title: MC0-02188
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated December 24, 2019, to reject their claims for refugee protection on the grounds that the appellants had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Campeche or Yucatan.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (principal appellant), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXand her son, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (associate appellants) are citizens of Mexico. They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated December 24, 2019, to reject their claims for refugee protection on the grounds that the appellants had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Campeche or Yucatan.
The appellants allege that the RPD erred in finding that they had an IFA in Mexico1 and that its analysis of the evidence was incomplete and erroneous.2
The appellants are asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow their appeal, set aside the RPD's determination and allow their claims for refugee protection.3
The determinative issue before the RAD is the same as the determinative issue before the RPD, namely, the IFA.
The RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

On his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the principal appellant, a taxi driver from the state of Guerrero, alleges that he had been receiving death threats from several people since XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, an individual threatened him with a weapon and stole his car.
In 2017, he learned that one of his brothers (XXXX) came to Canada to claim refugee protection.
In XXXX 2018, another one of his brothers (XXXX) was murdered. The principal appellant moved to Acapulco because of the threats he was receiving.
On XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, two individuals came to the principal appellant's house. They threatened him and told him that they would kill him if he did not leave the state of Guerrero.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, the principal appellant took a flight to Montréal and claimed protection in Canada.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, his wife, the female associate appellant, left Mexico and joined the appellant in Canada. She also claimed refugee protection, basing her claim on that of the principal appellant.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the son of the female associate appellant joined the appellants in Montréal, and he filed a claim for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. He alleges that individuals had come to his home on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, and asked him where his stepfather was.

The RAD reviews RPD decisions, applying the correctness standard of review after carrying out its own analysis of the record. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage with respect to the credibility assessment.4 That being said, the role of the RAD is to determine whether the RPD did indeed commit errors, as the appellants stated.
The RAD applied the correctness standard in this case.

In Rasaratnam5 and Thirunavukkarasu,6 the Federal Court of Appeal defined the criteria to apply in order to assess an IFA. It involves a two-pronged test: 1. ...the Board must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists.7 2. Conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.8
Both prongs must be satisfied in order to conclude that an IFA exists. First prong

The first prong must be examined from the perspective of the agent of persecution, namely, the agent of persecution's interest in following a refugee protection claimant to the area proposed as an IFA and their ability to find the claimant. Once those aspects have been analyzed, the claimant's personal circumstances and the circumstances of the people living in the IFA location must be considered. A) The criminals' interest in tracking down the appellants in Campeche or Yucatan

The RPD concluded that the incidents that occurred in the state of Guerrero (the murder of the principal appellant's brother and the threats made to his parents) do not show that these agents of harm have an interest in tracking down the appellants in Campeche or Yucatan.9

The RPD questioned the principal appellant about why his aggressors would be looking for him when he had complied with their demand and left the state of Guerrero. He stated that his aggressors might come looking for him in Campeche or Yucatan because they think he wants to avenge the death of his brother or because he filed a complaint in XXXX 2018.10

The RPD concluded that the principal appellant's answers were purely speculative. The RPD was of the opinion that these factors alone were not enough to reasonably explain, on a balance of probabilities, why the aggressors would still be interested in tracking down the appellants in Campeche or Yucatan, particularly since the complaint filed in XXXX 2018 does not accuse anyone in particular. It simply describes the threats received. Consequently, the RPD did not believe that the criminals would be interested in tracking down the appellants in the two locations suggested.11

The appellants argue that the XXXX family (the principal appellant's family) has been targeted for years,12 that they have been attacked by members of organized crime13 and that the parents are still being contacted by the agents of harm.14

The appellants argue that the interest of the agents of harm has changed over time, from the disappearance of one brother in 2012 to the threats currently being issued against the principal appellant's parents. Consequently, [translation] "it is obvious that the aggressors never lost interest in finding the appellants" and that they are more than likely still interested in tracking them down.15

Finally, the appellants submit that the RPD: 16 - did not exercise due diligence in justifying its findings and setting out its reasons for concluding that the attacks on the principal appellant's parents do not demonstrate that the aggressors are still interested in tracking down the appellants; - did not seem to take into consideration all of the facts presented by the appellants or changed the nature of those facts; - did not address the other threats received by the principal appellant and his brothers; - confused interest with ability by indicating that [translation] "the fact that the incidents occurred in the state of Guerrero shows a lack of interest in tracking down the appellants in Yucatan or Campeche."
The RAD disagrees.

First, there is nothing in the evidence or the appellants' testimony that makes it possible to identify the agents of persecution in order to be able to determine whether they have a particular interest in finding the appellants wherever they go in Mexico, particularly in Campeche or Yucatan.
Second, the burden of demonstrating such an interest falls on the refugee protection claimant, not on the RPD or the RAD.

Contrary to the appellants' counsel argument in paragraph 10 of the memorandum that members of XXXX family were attacked by organized crime, the RPD questioned the three appellants to find out whether they knew the agents of persecution and whether those agents belonged to known groups. They responded in the negative, as indicated in the following exchange:17 [translation] The RPD: So, XXXX XXXX XXXX, tell me who you are afraid of. The principal appellant: I'm afraid of the people who murdered my brother. The RPD: Do you know those people? The principal appellant: No, I don't know them. The RPD: Are they known by a nickname? The principal appellant: No. The RPD: Are you afraid of anyone other than the people who allegedly murdered your brother? The principal appellant: No. Just them. The RPD: And you, madam, who are you afraid of? The female associate appellant (XXXX XXXX XXXX): The people who murdered my brother-in-law. The RPD: And you, XXXX XXXX who are you afraid of? The male associate appellant (XXXX XXXX XXXX): I'm also afraid of the people who murdered his brother. The RPD: Madam and XXXX XXXX are you afraid of anyone else? The male associate appellant: No, just those people.
The RAD is of the opinion that the agents of harm have no interest in tracking down the appellants in a location that is very far away (over a thousand kilometres) for the following reasons:

The evidence presented in this case shows that all of the incidents alleged by the appellants happened in the state of Guerrero, whether it be the murder of the principal appellant's brother in the city of XXXX in 2018, the threats received by the principal appellant in 2018, the threats received by the male associate appellant, XXXX, in 2019 in Acapulco or those received by the parents of the principal appellant.

Furthermore, all of these incidents were committed by unidentified individuals for no apparent reason, according to the appellants' written account and testimony. In paragraph 14 of his written account, the principal appellant states: [translation] "On XXXX XXXX, I was threatened by two individuals who came to my home to tell me that they did not want to see me in the state again or I would end up like my brother XXXX." In paragraph 15 of the same account, he writes: [translation] "On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, the two individuals in question were waiting for me in front of my house with two other people. I tried to leave, but one of the men fired three shots in the air, and I felt paralyzed. He told me that if I did not leave, then the next bullet would be for me." [emphasis added]

The state of Guerrero on the west coast of Mexico (Pacific Ocean side) is 1,610 km from the state of Yucatan and 1,370 km from the state of Campeche, both of which are located on the east coast of Mexico. The principal appellant testified that all the agents of harm wanted him to do was to leave the Guerrero area and they would let him live. As a result, if the appellants were to move to one of the two suggested areas, which are located over 1,300 km away, it would take away any incentive their aggressors had to find them because they would be meeting the conditions set out by their aggressors.

The RAD is of the opinion that the appellants did not discharge their burden of establishing that the people they are afraid of have an interest in finding out that they moved to one of the proposed areas. The arguments raised in support of their position are speculative and are not objectively well founded enough to conclude otherwise. For all of the above-mentioned reasons, the RPD's conclusion is correct. B) The criminals' ability to find the appellants in Campeche or Yucatan

The RPD questioned the appellants about how the aggressors would track them down in Campeche or Yucatan. The principal appellant testified that he did not know how they would do that but that his name would be on the records as soon as he rented a place to live or requested public services such as electricity.18
The RPD concluded that the appellants did not show, on the balance of probabilities, that these men would be able to find them in the suggested areas.19

To that effect, the RPD noted that, at the beginning of the hearing, none of the appellants were able to give any information about the agents of persecution. The principal appellant testified that these men never identified themselves and that he did not know whether they belonged to a criminal organization.20

The RPD was therefore of the opinion that, because the appellants were unable to provide any information about these men, the appellants failed to demonstrate that the men would be able to track them down in Campeche or Yucatan, through records or other means.21

The appellants submit that the RPD erred by imposing on the appellants the heavy burden of having to know all of the details about the agents of harm in order to determine whether there is an IFA.22 The appellants argue that the fact that they do not know the identity of the aggressors does not mean that the aggressors will be unable to track them down, since the facts show that these aggressors are very organized, which implies that they do not belong to a local gang but are members of organized crime.23

The appellants note that the National Documentation Package (NDP) indicates that members of organized crime act with impunity, that they have infiltrated law enforcement agencies and that corruption is widespread to support their argument that it is likely they could be tracked down by members of organized crime anywhere in Mexico. If they were to return to Mexico, they will have to take administrative action that will leave traces that will make them easy to find.24
The RAD disagrees.

First, the argument of the appellants' counsel to the effect that the agents of persecution are members of organized crime in Mexico is purely speculative. The appellants themselves stated that they did not know anything about the subject, and none of them had any information about the aggressors.

Second, the RAD recognizes that corruption exists in Mexico and that organized crime is widespread in that county. However, the appellants did not provide sufficient evidence to show, on a balance of probabilities, that their agents of persecution have the means, ability, motivation and interest to track them down in Campeche or Yucatan.

As a result, the fear expressed by the appellants' counsel is completely hypothetical. The RPD took that fear into account but still rightly concluded that the appellants did not discharge the burden of establishing the risk required under the first prong of the IFA test.

Finally, the RAD is of the opinion that, with regard to the first prong of the IFA test, the evidence presented does not show that there is a serious possibility of persecution for the appellants or that there is a probability that they would be subjected to a risk to their life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or torture if they were to settle in one of the proposed states in Mexico. Second prong

The RPD concluded that the appellants simply raised the following concerns: that the agents of persecution would find them and that the principal appellant and female associate appellant would not be able to find employment. The RPD noted that the appellants had always worked in Mexico and the United States (for the principal appellant). Consequently, the RPD concluded that the appellants would all be able to resettle elsewhere, find work and meet their needs, whether it be in Campeche or in Yucatan.25

The appellants argue the following:26 - They do not have any family members or friends in the areas suggested so they will not have any support in relocating to those areas. - They are just a taxi driver and a woman without any education. - They had jobs in cities where they had support from family and friends. - The job situation in Mexico should not be compared to that in the United States.
The appellants submit that their removal to an unfamiliar city will be very distressing for them.27
The RAD cannot agree with the appellants' arguments and concludes that they are unfounded.

As indicated in the case law,28 there is a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable, considering the particular circumstances. This high standard requires proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and in living in the IFA location.29

The appellants' arguments to the effect that the RPD did not consider their personal circumstances cannot be accepted. The immigration forms of each appellant are sufficient to establish their respective occupations. The principal appellant is a taxi driver, his wife has always been able to work in the restaurant industry, and her son testified that he would be able to find a job. All of them speak Spanish, which is the language used in the proposed areas.

With regard to the argument that [translation] "it is not right to compare two completely different countries, such as the United States and Mexico," the RAD respectfully submits that the RPD did not compare the employment situation in the two countries. It simply noted that the principal appellant had always worked, both in Mexico and during his stay in the United States.

On his immigration form (IMM0008), the principal appellant indicated [translation] "Anything" for the type of employment he would do if his claim for refugee protection in Canada was allowed. The associate appellants both indicated [translation] "any reasonable employment" on their forms.

The claim that it would be unreasonable for the appellants to seek refuge in the proposed IFAs because it would cause them great distress and they would not be able to find a job they like does not meet the high threshold of the second prong of the IFA test.
It is not a matter of the claimant's convenience or the attractiveness of the IFA.30 The appellants had to establish on a balance of probabilities that the IFA would jeopardize their lives or safety.

The RPD concluded that the appellants [translation] "did not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for them to seek refuge in these cities, given the conditions in the proposed cities and all of the circumstances in this case, including their personal circumstances." The RAD agrees. The RPD's conclusion is correct.

The RPD's decision is correct. Consequently, considering all of the above, the RAD concludes that the appellants have failed to demonstrate that the RDP committed errors that would justify the RAD's intervention.

For these reasons, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or "persons in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
